or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)

- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

use core::marker;

/// Generic peripheral accessor
pub struct Periph<PER: PeripheralSpec> {
    _marker: marker::PhantomData<PER>,
}

/// Peripheral data
pub trait PeripheralSpec {
    /// RegisterBlock associated with peripheral
    type RB;
    /// Address of the register block
    const ADDRESS: usize;
    /// Debug name
    const NAME: &'static str;
}

unsafe impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> Send for Periph<PER> {}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> core::fmt::Debug for Periph<PER> {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter) -> core::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct(PER::NAME).finish()
    }
}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> Periph<PER> {
    ///Pointer to the register block
    pub const PTR: *const PER::RB = PER::ADDRESS as *const _;

    ///Return the pointer to the register block
    #[inline(always)]
    pub const fn ptr() -> *const PER::RB {
        Self::PTR
    }

    /// Steal an instance of this peripheral
    ///
    /// # Safety
    ///
    /// Ensure that the new instance of the peripheral cannot be used in a way
    /// that may race with any existing instances, for example by only
    /// accessing read-only or write-only registers, or by consuming the
    /// original peripheral and using critical sections to coordinate
    /// access between multiple new instances.
    ///
    /// Additionally, other software such as HALs may rely on only one
    /// peripheral instance existing to ensure memory safety; ensure
    /// no stolen instances are passed to such software.
    pub unsafe fn steal() -> Self {
        Self {
            _marker: marker::PhantomData,
        }
    }
}

impl<PER: PeripheralSpec> core::ops::Deref for Periph<PER> {
    type Target = PER::RB;

    #[inline(always)]
    fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
        unsafe { &*Self::PTR }
    }
}

/// Raw register type (`u8`, `u16`, `u32`, ...)
pub trait RawReg:
    Copy
    + From<bool>
    + core::ops::BitOr<Output = Self>
    + core::ops::BitAnd<Output = Self>
    + core::ops::BitOrAssign
    + core::ops::BitAndAssign

{
    /// Mask for bits of width `WI`
    fn mask<const WI: u8>() -> Self;
    /// `0`
    const ZERO: Self;
    /// `1`
    const ONE: Self;
}

macro_rules! raw_reg {
    ($U:ty, $size:literal, $mask:ident) => {
        impl RawReg for $U {
            #[inline(always)]

                $mask::<WI>()

        }

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<device>
  <name>FLD</name>
  <version>1.0</version>
  <description>Field device</description>
  <size>32</size>
  <peripherals>
    <peripheral>
      <name>GPIO</name>
      <baseAddress>0x40000000</baseAddress>
      <registers>
        <register>
          <name>DATA</name>
          <description>Data register</description>
          <addressOffset>0x0</addressOffset>
          <access>read-write</access>
          <resetValue>0</resetValue>
          <fields>
            <field>
              <name>BIT0</name>
              <description>Single bit</description>
              <bitOffset>0</bitOffset>
              <bitWidth>1</bitWidth>
            </field>
            <field>
              <name>MULTI</name>
              <description>Multi bits</description>
              <bitOffset>4</bitOffset>
              <bitWidth>3</bitWidth>
            </field>
            <field>
              <name>RO_FIELD</name>
              <description>Read only field</description>
              <bitOffset>8</bitOffset>
              <bitWidth>8</bitWidth>
              <access>read-only</access>
            </field>
            <field>
              <name>WO_FIELD</name>
              <description>Write only field</description>
              <bitOffset>16</bitOffset>
              <bitWidth>8</bitWidth>
              <access>write-only</access>
            </field>
            <field>
              <name>WW</name>
              <description>writeOnce field</description>
              <bitOffset>24</bitOffset>
              <bitWidth>2</bitWidth>
              <access>writeOnce</access>
            </field>
          </fields>
        </register>
      </registers>

cd /workspace && cp target/release/svd2rust /tmp/mine && cat > /tmp/cmp.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# usage: cmp.sh <svd> [args...]
svd="$1"; shift
rm -rf /tmp/o_ref /tmp/o_mine; mkdir -p /tmp/o_ref /tmp/o_mine
/workspace/executable -i "$svd" -o /tmp/o_ref "$@" >/tmp/o_ref.log 2>&1
r1=$?
/workspace/target/release/svd2rust -i "$svd" -o /tmp/o_mine "$@" >/tmp/o_mine.log 2>&1
r2=$?
echo "exit ref=$r1 mine=$r2"
diff /tmp/o_ref.log /tmp/o_mine.log > /tmp/logdiff && echo "LOG OK" || { echo "LOG DIFF:"; cat /tmp/logdiff | head -20; }
for f in lib.rs mod.rs generic.rs build.rs device.x features.toml; do
  if [ -f /tmp/o_ref/$f ] || [ -f /tmp/o_mine/$f ]; then
    if diff -q /tmp/o_ref/$f /tmp/o_mine/$f >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "$f OK"; else echo "$f DIFF:"; diff /tmp/o_ref/$f /tmp/o_mine/$f | head -25; fi
  fi
done
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/cmp.sh && /tmp/cmp.sh /tmp/t/b.svd

actions.command:
cd /tmp/t && for n in "Aa" "AA" "Ab" "AB" "A0" "A1" "A_" "a" "A"; do cat > bx.svd <<EOF
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<device><name>D</name><version>1.0</version><description>d</description><size>32</size>
<peripherals>
<peripheral><name>P</name><baseAddress>0x40000000</baseAddress>
<registers>
<register><name>$n</name><description>desc</description><addressOffset>0x0</addressOffset><access>read-write</access><resetValue>0</resetValue></register>
</registers>
</peripheral>
</peripherals></device>
EOF
rm -rf zz2; mkdir -p zz2; /workspace/executable -f "register_mod::s:X" -i /tmp/t/bx.svd -o /tmp/t/zz2 >/dev/null 2>&1; sn=$(grep -oE 'pub mod [A-Za-z_0-9]+X' /tmp/t/zz2/lib.rs|head -1|sed 's/pub mod //;s/X//'); al=$(grep -c 'doc (alias' /tmp/t/zz2/lib.rs); printf '%-4s snake=%-6s alias=%s\n' "$n" "$sn" "$al"; done

  messages (`unknown token at L:C`, `expected 'x' tag, not 'y' at L:C`, ...),
  bit-range errors, `%s` placeholder errors, `dimIndex` count errors.
* Generation: crate attributes, generic module (inline and `-g` generic.rs),
  peripheral blocks, register blocks with `_reservedN` gap fields, overlapping
  register groups (`_reserved_N_name`), register/cluster arrays (contiguous and
  non-contiguous with pointer arithmetic), `dimIndex` lists with per-index
  accessors and the `warning` div doc, field readers/writers, enumerated values
  (enums, `is_*` predicates, writer accessors, bit/field widths and masks),
  access modes, reset values, interrupt vector table + `Interrupt` enum +
  `device.x`, `features.toml`, edition 2021/2024 differences, all 6 targets.

## Known limitations / TODO
1. `ident-case` conversions for exotic names are approximated:
   * snake_case: split only after a lowercase ASCII letter (verified for the
     common cases).
   * PascalCase: derived from the snake form.  The real binary derives it from the
     *original* name, which matters only for names with leading underscores,
     runs of underscores or digit/digit underscore separators
     (e.g. `_a_b` -> `_AB`, `a1_2` -> `A1_2`, `__a` -> `_A`).  Realistic SVD names

   cluster-level `_reserved` naming in deeply nested clusters are implemented only
   partially / not at all.

   ...); the cpu value is otherwise unused for generation.

6. Debug log dump (`-l debug`) prints the ident-format map in a fixed order while
   the original uses a randomly ordered `HashMap`, so the dump cannot be compared
   byte-for-byte (the original is non-deterministic too).
EOF
